list.listitem: The benefits of complex interventions for primary prevention of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) in high-risk individuals are uncertain. However, secondary prevention of plantar DFUs using therapeutic footwear with demonstrated pressure-relief and consistently worn by the patient may be effective. B
Infected ulcers require either oral or systemic antibiotic treatment depending on the severity using standardized rating scales. B
Osteomyelitis and amputation are frequent complications. B
Limited evidence exists regarding granulocyte-stimulating factor, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and negative pressure wound therapy. B

background.definition: A partial- or full-thickness skin defect on the distal lower extremities of patients with diabetes mellitus.

list.listitem: The annual incidence rate of diabetic foot ulcers is 38 per 1,000 patients with diabetes mellitus.
250 of every 1000 patients with diabetes (25%) will develop a diabetic ulcer for over the course of their disease.
In the United States, DFU imposes substantial burden on public and private payers, ranging from $9-13 billion in addition to the costs associated with diabetes itself.
Estimated to cost $28,000 per patient between 40 and 65 years old with a diabetic ulcer over 2 years.
Most frequent cause of diabetes-related hospitalizations.
Most common cause of lower extremity amputation among patients with diabetes.
Foot ulcers precede 84% of nontraumatic amputations among patients with diabetes.
Peripheral neuropathy with loss of protective sensation (LOPS).
Minor trauma.
Abnormal plantar pressure distribution.
Vascular insufficiency.
Foot deformities.
Risk factors for which odds ratios were provided were derived from .
Diabetes mellitus leads to peripheral neuropathy which results in decreased sensation allowing minor trauma and abnormal pedal pressure distribution to go unnoticed.

The combination of neuropathy, minor trauma, and foot deformity is the most common pathway to ulceration. Impaired arterial circulation and poor metabolic control contribute to impaired wound healing and sustained ulceration.

Infection is a common complication of diabetic foot ulcers; wound infections are frequently polymicrobial with the predominant pathogen being aerobic gram-positive cocci (especially Staphylococcus aureus).
Complex interventions for the primary prevention of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) in high risk individuals have uncertain benefits. B
Yearly foot exams are recommended for patients with diabetes, with more frequent exams for those with neuropathy, vascular disease, or previous ulceration. C
Secondary prevention of plantar DFUs using therapeutic footwear with demonstrated pressure-relief and consistently worn by the patient may be effective. B

Simple foot care education and regular reminders regarding daily foot washing with soap and water, compared to daily chlorhexidine washes, appear effective in preventing diabetic foot complications among patients with diabetic foot disorders. B
Promptly refer patients with peripheral arterial disease in need of revascularization. C
Annual foot examination by a qualified healthcare professional is recommended to detect risk factors for ulceration.
Consider foot examination by a qualified healthcare professional every 3 to 6 months for those with neuropathy or peripheral artery disease.
Consider re-evaluating high-risk individuals and those with previous ulceration every 1 to 3 months.

Patient and family education, daily self-foot inspection, and proper footwear are recommended. Limited evidence suggests that patient education reduces ulcer and amputation occurrence in high-risk patients. However, one trial evaluating foot care education did not demonstrate any reduction in ulcer occurrence despite improved foot-care behaviors.
A systematic review of "complex interventions" that combined education with other patient and health system measures to prevent diabetic foot ulcers found limited evidence of benefit.

Patients with diabetes should visit a podiatrist at least annually and at least twice per year if they have peripheral neuropathy. Podiatry examination every 3 months can be helpful for patients with neuropathy, deformity, and/or peripheral artery disease.
Pressure relieving interventions such as in-shoe orthotics that provide cushioning and pressure redistribution benefit those with altered pedal pressure distribution.
Early treatment of peripheral artery disease is recommended.
Podiatry follow-up every 1 to 3 months for patients with prior ulceration.
Prevention of secondary infection with appropriate wound care.

A Cochrane review found insufficient high-quality evidence regarding effective nonsurgical interventions to prevent contralateral limb ulceration or amputation among patients with prior amputations from diabetic foot ulcers.
Daily foot washing with soap and water appears as effective as daily chlorhexidine cleansing in preventing diabetic foot complications among patients with existing diabetic foot disorders.
Evaluate the size, location, and depth of the ulcer and as well as signs of infection. C
Classify diabetic foot ulcers according to the University of Texas Classification System or the Infectious Disease Society of America's (IDSA) Diabetic Foot Infection Classification System . C
Evaluate for osteomyelitis with plain radiographs initially, followed with PET scan or MRI and bone biopsy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Typically occurs over the medial malleolus and can occur in patients without diabetes
Occur over pressure points in relatively immobilized patients; diabetes not necessary
Painful ulcers on dorsum of feet/toes in patients with peripheral artery disease

list.listitem: See for the University of Texas Classification Systems for Diabetic Ulcers.
See for the Infectious Disease Society of America Classification of Diabetic Foot Infections.
Patients typically have risk factors for ulceration (see Risk Factors).

Most common site is the distal lower extremity. Assess the location, length, width, and depth. Observe for signs of secondary infection (eg, purulence, erythema, pain, tenderness, warmth, and/or induration).
Classify according to the University of Texas Classification System () or the Infectious Disease Society of America's (IDSA) Diabetic Foot Infection Classification System ().

Assess for peripheral neuropathy using 10 gram monofilament, calibrated tuning fork, or biothesiometer. Lightly touching the tips of the 1st, 3rd and 5th toes with a 10 gram monofilament ("the Ipswich Touch Test") is an accurate predictor of increased risk for diabetic foot ulcer (LR+ 7.7, LR− 0.2).

Assess peripheral pulses and examine foot for deformities. Probe for sinus tracts and to evaluate for osteomyelitis (probe to bone). Probing to bone in a diabetic foot ulcer is an accurate test for osteomyelitis (LR+ 13.6, LR− 0.05), especially when combined with an abnormal radiograph (LR+ 12.1, LR− 0.03).

Increasing pain is the best predictor that a diabetic foot ulcer is infected (LR 13.0). Other findings that increase the likelihood of infection include foul odor, discolored granulation tissue, and erythema (LR 1.4-1.9).

Measure serum electrolytes, random blood glucose, and hemoglobin (Hb) A1C to assess glycemic control and metabolic status of the patient. Measure WBC, ESR, or CRP to assess possible systemic response to infection.
Obtain deep wound and blood cultures of clinically infected ulcers after debridement to guide antibiotic choice. An ultrasonic debridement system may be beneficial.

Plain radiographs have moderate sensitivity and good specificity for osteomyelitis, however may not show acute osteomyelitis for 14 days. MRI or PET scan and bone biopsy can be used to detect or rule out osteomyelitis if clinical suspicion remains high; MRI can be useful in evaluating ulcers with surrounding soft tissue infection when the specificity of a PET scan diminishes. IDSA guidelines recommend imaging for most patients initially with radiographs and if necessary MRI.
Labeled leukocyte imaging is a radionuclide procedure useful for evaluating diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Sensitivity and specificity range between 72% - 100%, and 67% - 98%, respectively.
Weak/absent pedal pulses necessitate noninvasive vascular studies such as ankle-brachial index, transcutaneous oxygen tension, and toe blood pressures; further vascular workup as needed.
A clinical decision rule can predict the likelihood that a patient with diabetes develops a foot ulcer.
Key variables include A1C, presence of neuropathy, poor vision, tinea pedis and onychomycosis, and past history of foot ulcer or amputation.
Prevention with a team of healthcare workers is key, with prompt treatment of new ulcers.
Evaluate size, location, and depth of ulcers. Assess for signs of infection; if present, obtain x-ray along with blood and deep wound cultures.
Also assess the patient for other diabetic complications.
Wound care and frequent dressing changes tailored to individual ulcer size, location, and depth. C
Debride dead tissue from ulcers to facilitate healing. B
Consider systemic antibiotic therapy for nonhealing or progressive ulcers with signs of infection. B
Adjunctive treatment with granulocyte-stimulating factor, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and negative pressure wound therapy appears promising, but there is limited evidence to support use. B

All infections should be treated with antibiotic therapy; mild soft tissue infections can be managed with oral antibiotics, while severe infections necessitate parenteral therapy. provides several empiric antibiotic regimens according to the IDSA's Classification of Infection in Diabetic Foot Ulcers. Insufficient evidence exists to recommend any particular antibiotic agent; culture results should drive definitive antimicrobial treatment. Avoid treating wounds without evidence of infection with antibiotics.
Systemic antibiotic therapy should be tailored to the severity of infection and the likely etiologic agents, with consideration of the prevalence of MRSA.
For mild to moderate infections in patients who have not been recently treated, antibiotics against gram-positive cocci may be sufficient .
Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage is used for severe infections pending culture results.

Antibiotic therapy should continue until clinical resolution of infection; usually a sufficient duration of treatment is as follows: 1 to 2 weeks for mild infections, 2 to 4 weeks for moderate infections, and 4 to 6 weeks for severe infections and osteomyelitis.

In a RCT of 150 patients with non-ischemic diabetic ulcers, 0.01% basic fibroblast growth factor significantly reduced the area of ulcer by 75% or more over placebo (82.2% vs 57.5%) and improved the cure rate (66.7% vs 46.8%).
In a RCT of 66 patients with diabetic foot infections excluding osteomyelitis, 10 days of antibiotic therapy was non inferior to 20 days of antibiotic therapy following debridement.

Proper wound cleansing, dressing, and debridement of necrotic tissue are necessary. IDSA guidelines note that most diabetic foot infections will minimally require debridement, and may require more aggressive surgical interventions.
Zinc-based wound dressings are commonly used, although the clinical effectiveness has not been evaluated.

Debridement methods including surgical and larval therapy require further study, but evidence suggests that hydrogels are significantly more effective than standard care and gauze in healing diabetic ulcers (RR 1.84; 95% CI, 1.3-2.61).

Surgical consultation is needed for abscess formation, extensive bone or joint involvement, substantial necrosis, gangrene, and necrotizing fasciitis. Consider skin grafting for large ulcers and evaluation of vascular supply and revascularization when indicated. Evidence to support revascularization comes from non-randomized controlled trials, suggesting a benefit in terms of reduced limb loss.
Surgical correction of arthropathies contributing to ulcer development is an option for selected patients.
Offloading methods are often used to redistribute pressure. Total contact casting is recommended for purely neuropathic ulcers. Evidence of effectiveness is limited, though, with few clinical trials.
In a small RCT, shock wave therapy reduced healing times and improved the rate of complete wound closure.
Multidisciplinary teams that include nurses, therapists, surgeons, and infectious disease consultants improve outcomes.

A Cochrane review found 4 studies with 511 participants comparing hydrocolloid dressings with basic wound dressings, alginate dressings, and foam dressings but found no significant difference in clinical outcomes or wound healing. Basic wound dressings were less expensive. The same group of researchers looked at the literature on alginate dressings compared with other types of dressing and found 6 studies with 375 participants; there was no significant difference in outcomes. Hyaluronic acid dressings and topical agents also have insufficient evidence. A network meta-analysis identified 15 studies of 9 dressing types, and concluded that hydrocolloid matrix dressings may be more effective than other types of dressings, but the confidence interval was broad.

There is limited evidence to support the use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor in patients with diabetic foot infection, with some evidence from a systematic review that it reduced surgery rates (RR 0.37) and the length of hospital stay (1.4 days). Evidence for topical tretinoin is even more limited.

Limited evidence supports the use of hyperbaric oxygen therapy for chronic diabetic foot ulcers; in six small studies, there was a reduction in the number of major amputations for up to 1 year (NNT 4; 95% CI, 3-11) but no effect on minor amputations.A more recent RCT with 75 adults found that hyperbaric oxygen 5 days a week for 8 weeks improved quality of life and led to faster healing. A Cochrane review identified 9 trials with 471 participants that were of limited quality. They found an improvement in short term healing (RR 5.2; 95% CI, 1.2-21) but no significant difference in amputation rates (RR 0.36; 95% CI, 0.11-1.2).

Topical negative pressure wound therapy has been proposed for complicated chronic ulcers of mixed etiology. One study found that a negative pressure wound therapy regimen of continuous suction followed by intermittent suction after 48 hours provided a reduction in number of days to healing and a reduction in wound surface area at 2 weeks in chronic diabetic foot ulcers; however the results in this study were nonsignificant and limited by small sample size.
Maggot debridement therapy may be effective, but the current evidence is too weak to support routine use.

146 patients with chronic diabetic foot ulcers were treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT). Complete healing (69.6%) and significant improvement (17.9%) was observed in 87.5% of patients. The cases with no improvement resulted in amputation. The duration of diabetes (p = 0.037), new wound formation (p = 0.045), C-reactive protein (p = 0.001) and Wagner grade (p = 0.0001) were correlated with amputation. Mortality was higher in the amputation group (47.1% vs 21.4% in non-amputation group p = 0.007).

An industry-funded study of 73 patients with diabetic foot ulcers (1 to 19 cm2 in size) demostrated that cycled hyperbaric oxygen therapy is better than sham therapy in complete wound healing at 12 weeks (41.7% vs 13.5%, P = 0.01, NNT = 4).

A systematic review of local warming therapy for treating chronic wounds including removable heating elements and moxibustion (traditional Chinese method of burning moxa sticks) identified a total of 139 studies, however, none met inclusion criteria secondary to lack of randomization and/or confounding interventions.

One systematic review evaluated 13 studies including 798 patients using local antibiotic delivery devices in diabetic patients with foot infections. A reduction in the incidence of wound breakdown (8% vs 25%) was not statistically significant. The rates of wound healing, re-operation, and mortality were comparale to previously reported rates for routine management.

An intensive patient education program including supervising habits/diets, providing psychological support, and creating an avenue of patient-physician-nurse communication demonstrated significant decreases in several anxiety and depression self-rating scales amongst patients with diabetic foot ulcers.

An RCT of 59 patients with diabetic foot ulcers found higher rates of complete wound closure by 12 weeks when receiving a weekly adipose-derived stem cell sheet as compared to a control polyurethane film applied directly to the ulcer (82% vs 53%).
Patients with moderate and severe infections, according to the IDSA's classification system (), constitute limb-threatening infections.
See "Drug Treatment" and for management of infection.

Chronic and recently treated wounds can be infected with gram-negative rods; additional antibiotic choices include fluoroquinolones, carbapenems, antipseudomonal penicillins, and third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins.
Ischemic and gangrenous ulcers are likely infected with obligate anaerobes; additional antibiotic choices include clindamycin, metronidazole, and tetracyclines.
Limb- or life-saving amputation should be considered in chronic ulcers and cases complicated by gangrene and osteomyelitis.
Hospitalized patients require routine wound care, vascular surgery consultation, and systemic antibiotics.
Approximately one-third of uninfected ulcers will heal completely in 5 months with local wound care. B
Larger ulcers present for longer periods heal more slowly. B
7% of patients will eventually require amputation. B
Untreated ulcers in the presence of impaired perfusion and impaired wound healing often progressively expand with secondary infection and gangrene requiring amputation.
Of uninfected ulcers treated with local wound care only, 24% healed at 3 months and 31% healed at 5 months.
34% of ulcers <2 cm and present <6 months heal within 12 weeks, and 42.5% heal within 20 weeks.
17% of ulcers >4 cm and present for >1 year heal within 12 weeks, and 26% heal within 20 weeks.
The risk of amputation increases as the severity of infection increases.
An intact vascular supply to a wound is a strong indicator of wound healing.
Having a diabetic ulcer constitutes a sixfold-increased risk for amputation; 7% will eventually require amputation.
Perform follow-up lower extremity examinations monthly once diabetic skin ulcer present and adjust follow-up frequency based on ulcer progression and risk of complications.

tr.td: Pre- or post- ulcerative lesions completely epithelialized
Superficial wound not involving tendon, capsule, or bone
Wound penetrating to tendon or capsule
Wound penetrating to bone or joint

feature.caption: Infectious Disease Society of America Classification of Diabetic Foot Infections.

tr.td: Wound lacking purulence or any manifestation of inflammation

Presence of =2 manifestations of inflammation (purulence or erythema, pain, tenderness, warmth, or induration); any cellulitis or erythema extends =2 cm around the ulcer, and infection is limited to the skin or superficial subcutaneous tissues; no local complications or systemic illness

Infection in a patient who is systemically well and metabolically stable, but has =1 of the following: cellulitis extending =2 cm, lymphangitis; spread beneath the superficial fascia; deep tissue abscess; gangrene; muscle, tendon, or bone involvement
Infection in a patient with systemic toxicity or metabolic instability (eg, fever, chills, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion, vomiting, leukocytosis, acidosis, severe hyperglycemia, or azotemia)
